examples.title: Cargo conservation
examples.setup: Two units × five vehicles. Each unit has control, three cargo trucks and recovery. Only the six cargo trucks carry 5 tonnes each.
examples.formula: L=\sum c_i,\quad D=\sum D_i,\quad X=\sum(1-a_i)(c_i-D_i),\quad I=\sum a_i(c_i-D_i)
steps: Load: 6 cargo trucks × 5 t = 30 t; control/recovery carry zero.
Deliver: 2 trucks × 5 t = 10 t. Remaining undelivered cargo is 20 t.
Force destruction of 2 different loaded trucks: X = 2 × 5 = 10 t.
Two living undelivered trucks remain: I = 2 × 5 = 10 t. Check 30 = 10 + 10 + 10; delivered fraction = 10/30 = 1/3.
examples.limit: The test assigns delivery/destruction states directly. The six glyphs represent cargo trucks only; their drawn positions and transitions are explanatory, not simulated travel.
examples.source_code:
def test_cargo_conservation_invariant():
    """At every point, C_loaded = C_delivered + C_lost + C_in_transit."""
    # 2 march units of 5 vehicles = 10 vehicles total
    # Roles per unit: 1 control, 3 cargo, 1 recovery => 6 cargo trucks total
    roles = ["control", "cargo", "cargo", "cargo", "recovery"]
    scn = _make_convoy_scenario(
        march_unit_size=5,
        march_units_per_serial=2,
        cargo_per_vehicle=5.0,
        roles=roles,
    )
    rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
    ent = build_entities(scn, rng)

    assert ent.n == 10
    assert int((ent.convoy_role == ROLE_CARGO).sum()) == 6
    assert float(ent.cargo[ent.convoy_role == ROLE_CARGO].sum()) == 30.0
    assert float(ent.cargo[ent.convoy_role == ROLE_CONTROL].sum()) == 0.0
    assert float(ent.cargo[ent.convoy_role == ROLE_RECOVERY].sum()) == 0.0

    c_loaded = float(ent.cargo[ent.side == BLUE].sum())
    assert c_loaded == 30.0

    # Simulate intermediate state:
    # 2 cargo trucks delivered (10 tons)
    # 2 cargo trucks destroyed (10 tons)
    # 2 cargo trucks in transit (10 tons)
    cargo_indices = np.where(ent.convoy_role == ROLE_CARGO)[0]
    delivered_idx = cargo_indices[:2]
    dead_idx = cargo_indices[2:4]
    transit_idx = cargo_indices[4:]
    assert len(transit_idx) == 2

    for idx in delivered_idx:
        ent.cargo_delivered[idx] = ent.cargo[idx]
    for idx in dead_idx:
        ent.alive[idx] = 0

    init_counts = {BLUE: 10, 1: 0}
    res = metrics.compute(scn, init_counts, ent, t_reached=100.0, t_elapsed=100.0)

    assert res["cargo_loaded"] == 30.0
    assert res["cargo_delivered"] == 10.0
    assert res["cargo_lost"] == 10.0
    assert res["cargo_in_transit"] == 10.0
    assert abs(res["cargo_loaded"] - (res["cargo_delivered"] + res["cargo_lost"] + res["cargo_in_transit"])) < 1e-6
    assert pytest.approx(res["delivered_frac"], 1e-6) == 10.0 / 30.0

examples.title: Halt and timed release
examples.setup: A receive-fire signal is supplied at step 0. clear_s=5 and dt=1 s. Signals are cleared for steps 1–5, then supplied again at step 6.
steps: k=0: receive_fire=true, so k_last=0 and 0−0=0<5. Hold activates.
k=1,2,3,4: no new trigger; elapsed values 1,2,3,4 are all less than 5. Hold remains active.
k=5: elapsed=5; 5<5 is false. Hold clears and contact ends.
k=6: a new receive-fire trigger starts a second contact episode; contact_count=2.
examples.limit: This is a behavior-state test, not a full movement or Herringbone test. Five representative glyphs stand for the held column; the test does not assert their travel distances.
examples.source_code:
def test_halt_holds_column_then_times_out():
    scn, ent, bhv = _convoy_state(["receive_fire"], release={"rule": "timeout", "clear_s": 5.0})
    bhv.fired_at[3] = True
    assert _step(scn, ent, bhv, 0).any()
    bhv.fired_at[:] = False
    for k in range(1, 5):
        assert _step(scn, ent, bhv, k).any()        # still inside the 5 s window
    assert not _step(scn, ent, bhv, 5).any() and not bhv.in_contact
    bhv.fired_at[3] = True                          # a fresh trigger is a second contact
    _step(scn, ent, bhv, 6)
    assert bhv.contact_count == 2

examples.title: Arc length on an L-shaped road
steps: First segment length: sqrt((1000−0)²+0²)=1000 m. Second segment length: 1000 m. Total=2000 m.
At s=500 m, remain on the first segment: r(500)=(500,0), heading=0.
At s=1500 m, pass the first 1000 m and travel 500 m along the second: r(1500)=(1000,500), heading=π/2.
Project (1050,600) onto x=1000: foot=(1000,600), s=1000+600=1600 m, cross-track distance=50 m.
examples.limit: The marker visits query positions from the geometry test. Interpolation is a teaching animation, not execution of vehicle motion.
examples.source_code:
def test_route_polyline_geometry_and_projection():
    """Verify cumulative distance, point_at, and orthogonal projection on an L-dogleg."""
    # L-dogleg: (0, 0) -> (1000, 0) -> (1000, 1000)
    pts = [(0.0, 0.0), (1000.0, 0.0), (1000.0, 1000.0)]
    r = RoutePolyline.from_waypoints(pts)

    assert r.total_length == pytest.approx(2000.0)
    assert np.allclose(r.cum_dist, [0.0, 1000.0, 2000.0])

    # Midpoint of first segment
    x, y, th = r.point_at(500.0)
    assert (x, y) == pytest.approx((500.0, 0.0))
    assert th == pytest.approx(0.0)

    # Midpoint of second segment (heading North = pi/2)
    x, y, th = r.point_at(1500.0)
    assert (x, y) == pytest.approx((1000.0, 500.0))
    assert th == pytest.approx(np.pi / 2)

    # Invertibility: project(point_at(s)) == s for any s in [0, L]
    for s_test in [0.0, 250.0, 999.0, 1000.0, 1001.0, 1750.0, 2000.0]:
        px, py, _ = r.point_at(s_test)
        s_proj, d_perp = r.project(px, py)
        assert s_proj == pytest.approx(s_test, abs=1e-6)
        assert d_perp == pytest.approx(0.0, abs=1e-6)

    # Off-route point orthogonal projection
    # Point at (500, 25): 25m lateral offset from first segment
    s_proj, d_perp = r.project(500.0, 25.0)
    assert s_proj == pytest.approx(500.0)
    assert d_perp == pytest.approx(25.0)

    # Point at (1050, 600): 50m lateral offset from second segment
    s_proj, d_perp = r.project(1050.0, 600.0)
    assert s_proj == pytest.approx(1600.0)
    assert d_perp == pytest.approx(50.0)

examples.title: Crew counts with escorts
examples.setup: Three units of five core vehicles, plus three armed escorts. Manned control/cargo crew=2; escort crew=3. Autonomous cargo crew=0.
steps: Core organization: 3 units × 5 vehicles = 15 vehicles, comprising 3 control vehicles and 12 cargo trucks.
Manned case: 15 × 2 + 3 × 3 = 30 + 9 = 39 people.
Autonomous-cargo case: 3 × 2 + 12 × 0 + 3 × 3 = 6 + 0 + 9 = 15 people.
Ratio: 39/15=2.6. Difference: 39−15=24 fewer onboard people. This is crew assignment, not evidence of fewer casualties.
examples.limit: This test also checks five escorts (45 versus 21 crew); this worked example covers only the three-escort subcase. It does not calculate exposure or casualty probability.
examples.source_code:
def test_reference_convoy_with_escorts():
    """Reference convoy with 3 and 5 escorts (ATP 4-11 G-8 equal cargo):
    3 escorts: manned 39, autonomous 15 (ratio 2.6).
    5 escorts: manned 45, autonomous 21 (ratio 2.14).
    """
    unit = {"march_unit_size": 5, "march_units_per_serial": 3, "serials_per_column": 1}
    # 3 escorts
    spec_m3 = {**unit, "autonomy_arm": "manned", "escort_vehicles": 3}
    spec_a3 = {**unit, "autonomy_arm": "autonomous_march_unit", "escort_vehicles": 3}
    ent_m3 = build_entities(SC.with_params({"convoy": spec_m3}), make_rng(0, SC.id))
    ent_a3 = build_entities(SC.with_params({"convoy": spec_a3}), make_rng(0, SC.id))
    m3 = int(ent_m3.crew[ent_m3.side == BLUE].sum())
    a3 = int(ent_a3.crew[ent_a3.side == BLUE].sum())
    assert m3 == 39
    assert a3 == 15
    assert m3 / a3 == 2.6

    # 5 escorts
    spec_m5 = {**unit, "autonomy_arm": "manned", "escort_vehicles": 5}
    spec_a5 = {**unit, "autonomy_arm": "autonomous_march_unit", "escort_vehicles": 5}
    ent_m5 = build_entities(SC.with_params({"convoy": spec_m5}), make_rng(0, SC.id))
    ent_a5 = build_entities(SC.with_params({"convoy": spec_a5}), make_rng(0, SC.id))
    m5 = int(ent_m5.crew[ent_m5.side == BLUE].sum())
    a5 = int(ent_a5.crew[ent_a5.side == BLUE].sum())
    assert m5 == 45
    assert a5 == 21
    assert round(m5 / a5, 2) == 2.14

examples.title: An explicit road-space penalty
examples.setup: The test uses success=1, time=500 s, Blue loss fraction=0.1 and road space=1000 m. Defaults: w_fail=1, w_time=0.3, w_loss=0.5, time_scale=1800 s.
steps: Enable w_road=0.2: added penalty=0.2×(1000/1000)=0.2.
New score: 0.133333…+0.2=0.333333…; the asserted score increase is exactly 0.2.
At RS=2000 m, penalty=0.2×2=0.4, giving J=0.533333…; higher is worse for this minimization score.
examples.limit: This verifies a configurable objective term, not optimization or a best policy. Drawn spacing is schematic; the test supplies road-space summary values directly.
examples.source_code:
def test_mission_score_road_space_penalty():
    """MissionScoreMetric penalizes road space when w_road > 0."""
    base_output = {
        "success_rate": 1.0,
        "time_to_objective": 500.0,
        "blue_loss_frac": 0.1,
        "convoy_road_space": 1000.0,
    }

    # Baseline with w_road = 0.0 (unchanged)
    m_default = MissionScoreMetric()
    score_default = float(m_default.compute(base_output)[0])

    # With road space penalty w_road = 0.2, road_scale = 1000.0
    m_road = MissionScoreMetric(w_road=0.2, road_scale=1000.0)
    score_road = float(m_road.compute(base_output)[0])

    # Expected addition: 0.2 * (1000.0 / 1000.0) = 0.2
    assert score_road == pytest.approx(score_default + 0.2)

    # Larger road space yields worse (higher) score
    score_larger = float(m_road.compute({**base_output, "convoy_road_space": 2000.0})[0])
    assert score_larger > score_road

examples.title: A building blocks one ray
examples.setup: World: 1000×1000 m, 25 m raster cells. Building cells [16:24,16:24] occupy the central 400–600 m block.
examples.formula: LOS=1[\text{no sampled ray point intersects a building}]
steps: Raster bounds: 16×25=400 m and 24×25=600 m; cells 16 through 23 are occupied.
Ray (200,500)→(800,500) crosses the building at y=500. Expected LOS=false.
Ray (200,200)→(800,200) stays below the building. Expected LOS=true.
Ray (100,100)→(200,100) also avoids the building. Assert [false,true,true].
examples.limit: The ray is animated for explanation. LOS is calculated by the raster model; this test does not validate radio propagation or probability of detection.
examples.source_code:
def test_building_los_blocking():
    """Verify vectorized World.los ray-marching accurately detects building occlusions."""
    ny, nx = 40, 40
    cell = 25.0
    world = World(
        size=(1000.0, 1000.0),
        cell=cell,
        speed=np.ones((ny, nx)),
        cover=np.zeros((ny, nx)),
        conceal=np.zeros((ny, nx)),
        buildings=np.zeros((ny, nx), dtype=bool),
    )

    # Place a building block from x in [400, 600], y in [400, 600]
    # In raster indices: ix in [16, 24], iy in [16, 24]
    world.buildings[16:24, 16:24] = True

    # Ray 1: Passes straight through building center from (200, 500) to (800, 500) -> BLOCKED
    # Ray 2: Runs parallel outside building from (200, 200) to (800, 200) -> CLEAR
    # Ray 3: Short ray inside street from (100, 100) to (200, 100) -> CLEAR
    x0 = np.array([200.0, 200.0, 100.0])
    y0 = np.array([500.0, 200.0, 100.0])
    x1 = np.array([800.0, 800.0, 200.0])
    y1 = np.array([500.0, 200.0, 100.0])

    clear = world.los(x0, y0, x1, y1)
    assert clear.shape == (3,)
    assert bool(clear[0]) is False
    assert bool(clear[1]) is True
    assert bool(clear[2]) is True

    # Test 2D broadcast (2, 2)
    b_clear = world.los(x0[:2, None], y0[:2, None], x1[None, :2], y1[None, :2])
    assert b_clear.shape == (2, 2)

examples.title: Promotion after three steps
examples.setup: The first unit head is deliberately marked dead. leader_loss_policy=promote and handoff_steps=3.
steps: Before tick 0, mark the unit head dead. This is a forced state change, not an enemy kill.
Ticks 0,1,2: no handoff yet. The first survivor still references the dead head; leaderless_steps accumulates to 3.
Tick 3: the configured delay is reached. Promote the first eligible survivor.
Assert: the new head has leader=−1, the unit head points to that survivor, and ll_handoffs=1.
examples.limit: Glyph colors show leadership status, not physical halt commands. This unit test does not prove the superiority of promotion or transfer any console.
examples.source_code:
def test_promote_latency():
    scn, ent, bhv = _state(_pol("promote", handoff_steps=3))
    u = _unit0(ent)
    ent.alive[u[0]] = False
    for k in range(3):
        _tick(scn, ent, bhv, k)
        assert ent.leader[u[1]] == u[0]          # still pointing at the dead head
    assert bhv.leaderless_steps == 3
    _tick(scn, ent, bhv, 3)
    assert ent.leader[u[1]] == -1 and bhv.ll_handoffs == 1 and bhv.ll_head[0] == u[1]

examples.title: Priority respects eligibility
examples.setup: New dedicated selector diagnostic: Red at x=0, cargo at x=40, control at x=100. The fixture initially declares both Blue targets eligible.
examples.formula: t^*=\arg\min_{i\in E\cap Control}d_i;\quad\text{if empty, use nearest eligible}
steps: Distances: d_cargo=|40−0|=40 m; d_control=|100−0|=100 m. Nearest eligible is cargo.
With order=[control] and both eligible, the control set is nonempty. Select the control at 100 m.
Change the supplied eligibility mask: control becomes ineligible.
The control set is now empty. Fall back to cargo at 40 m; priority cannot restore an ineligible target.
examples.limit: This new test calls the preserved branch selector used by the study. It supplies eligibility directly; it does not simulate sensing, LOS, firing or kill draws.
examples.source_code:
def test_control_priority_and_ineligible_fallback():
    path=Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]/'red_priority_18/branch_sources/target_priority.py'
    spec=importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('worked_target_priority',path)
    module=importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec);sys.modules[spec.name]=module;spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    ent=Entities.allocate(3)
    ent.side[:]=[BLUE,BLUE,RED];ent.convoy_role[:]=[0,1,-1]
    ent.x[:]=[100,40,0];ent.y[:]=0
    scn=SimpleNamespace(params={'target_priority':{'order':['control']}},objective=SimpleNamespace(goal=(200,0)))
    prio=module.build_target_priority(scn,ent)
    distance=np.abs(ent.x[:,None]-ent.x[None,:])
    eligible=np.zeros((3,3),bool);eligible[2,:2]=True
    target,_=module.select(ent,prio,eligible,distance,np.array([2]),np.array([1]))
    assert target.tolist()==[0]  # control at 100 m, despite cargo being nearer at 40 m
    eligible[2,0]=False
    target,_=module.select(ent,prio,eligible,distance,np.array([2]),np.array([1]))
    assert target.tolist()==[1]  # priority never restores an ineligible target

examples.title: Attention and served quality
examples.setup: Use one parameterized test case: four assigned crewless followers per console, span_capacity=2, q_auto=0.70 and q_operator=0.95.
steps: Count N=4 assigned followers per console. The selected test case sets capacity C=2.
Attention A=min(1,C/N)=min(1,2/4)=0.5.
Quality gain q_operator−q_auto=0.95−0.70=0.25; diluted gain=0.25×0.5=0.125.
Served quality q=0.70+0.125=0.825 for each of the three consoles. Other tested capacities 8,4,1 give attention 1,1,0.25.
examples.limit: This verifies the attention equation, not human workload calibration. The animation depicts one console; the assertion covers all three. Attention does not by itself change service time.
